bill.title: Bottles and Breastfeeding Equipment Screening Enhancement Act
bill.latestActionText: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 161.
bill.officialSummary: Bottles and Breastfeeding Equipment Screening Enhancement Act This bill directs the Transportation Security Administration to issue or update guidance to minimize the risk for contamination of breast milk, baby formula, purified deionized water for infants, juice, and related products that are subject to re-screening or additional screening, including by ensuring adherence to hygienic standards. Related products include ice packs, freezer packs, frozen gel packs, and other accessories required to cool breast milk, baby formula, and juice. In addition, the bill directs the Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General to audit compliance with these requirements and submit a report to Congress.

classification.plainSummary: This bill requires the Transportation Security Administration to create or update guidance for screening breast milk, baby formula, and related items at airports in ways that reduce contamination risk and follow hygiene standards. It also directs the Department of Homeland Security's inspector general to audit whether TSA is following these requirements and report the findings to Congress.

industries.rationale: The bill imposes new screening protocols and compliance obligations on TSA airport security operations.
Manufacturers of breast pumps, baby bottles, and related feeding equipment may face indirect effects from changed screening procedures.

plain.whatItDoes: This bill would order the Transportation Security Administration to issue or update guidance to minimize the risk for contamination of breast milk, baby formula, purified deionized water for infants, juice, and related products that are subject to re-screening or additional screening, including by ensuring adherence to hygienic standards.
plain.whoItTouches: Parents of young children. Children, and the adults responsible for them.
plain.everydayEffect: If it passed, the change would show up in a child's care. Nothing has changed yet. Most bills never become law.
plain.source: Reworded from the official summary. Staff at the Congressional Research Service wrote that summary. It is public domain, and the full text of it is further down this page.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
